opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that the model and the system are no longer separable problems. In the earlier days of deep learning, you could have one group of people designing architectures and another group building the frameworks and kernels, and they could mostly work independently. The models were small enough that, even if the system was a bit inefficient, you could still train and run them.

In the large-model era, that's no longer true. When you're training something at the scale of thousands of GPUs, or serving a model to millions of users, every inefficiency gets multiplied enormously. Whether an idea is viable often depends on whether it can be implemented efficiently on the hardware we actually have. A lot of the architectural choices that ended up winning, attention variants, mixture-of-experts, quantization-friendly designs, long-context techniques, succeeded partly because they mapped well onto the hardware and the software stack. So the system shapes what models are possible.

It goes the other way too. The workloads are changing really quickly. Things like KV cache management, speculative decoding, structured generation, and agentic workloads with many interleaved calls all put new demands on the system. If you build the system without understanding where the models are heading, you end up optimizing for yesterday's problem.

There's also the hardware diversity piece, which I care about a lot. We want these models to run not only in big data centers but also on laptops, phones, and in the browser. That requires thinking about the model, compiler, and runtime together. Projects like TVM and MLC came from that motivation: making it possible to bring a model efficiently to many different devices without hand-writing everything from scratch.

So for me, co-design isn't just about squeezing out performance. It's about expanding what's possible. When people who understand models and people who understand systems work closely together, or ideally when the same people think about both, you find solutions that neither side would find alone. I think that's where a lot of the most exciting progress in AI is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response says architectural ideas must map efficiently to available hardware and describes training at thousands of GPUs, clearly tying model design to GPU execution efficiency.

r002.rationale: It explains that large-scale training and serving magnify system inefficiencies and that model viability depends on efficient implementation, identifying systems support as necessary for scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that in the large-model era, the model and the system are no longer separable problems. For a long time we could pretend they were. Researchers would design an architecture, hand it to engineers, and the engineers would figure out how to run it. That worked when the models were small enough that the hardware had slack. Today there is no slack. Every frontier model is pushing right up against memory bandwidth, interconnect, and the cost of serving. So the decisions you make at the model level directly determine what is even possible at the system level, and vice versa.

Let me give a few concrete examples of what I mean. Take attention. The original formulation of attention is quadratic in sequence length, and if you treat that as a fixed mathematical object and just try to optimize the kernels, you hit a wall. The breakthroughs came from people who understood both the math and the memory hierarchy. FlashAttention is really a systems insight expressed as an algorithm. It did not change what attention computes, but it changed how it is computed in a way that only makes sense if you know how GPU SRAM and HBM interact. The same thing is true for things like grouped-query attention or multi-latent attention. Those are model design choices motivated almost entirely by the cost of the KV cache during inference. Someone designing the model had to be thinking about serving.

Mixture-of-experts is another good case. From a pure modeling perspective, MoE is attractive because you get more parameters for the same compute. But whether MoE actually makes sense depends entirely on your system. How many experts can you fit on a device? What does the all-to-all communication look like? Can you balance the load? If you design the model without understanding those constraints, you get something that looks great on paper and is miserable to run. And if you only work on the systems side, you keep trying to optimize an architecture that could have been designed to be easier to serve in the first place.

The second reason co-design matters is that the hardware landscape is fragmenting. It used to be that you targeted NVIDIA and that was mostly the story. Now you have multiple GPU vendors, custom accelerators, Apple silicon, mobile and edge devices, and people genuinely want to run these models everywhere. That was a big motivation for us in projects like TVM and MLC LLM. You cannot hand-write kernels for every model on every piece of hardware. You need a layer of abstraction that lets you express the model once and compile it efficiently to many targets. But building that layer well requires knowing what the models actually need, which again means the people doing compilers and the people doing modeling have to talk to each other constantly.

The third reason is that the cost structure has changed. Training a frontier model is enormously expensive, and inference at scale is now often the dominant cost. When a one-percent efficiency gain translates into millions of dollars, or into the difference between a feature being viable or not, you cannot afford to leave performance on the table because of a mismatch between the algorithm and the system. Things like speculative decoding, quantization schemes, paged attention for KV caches, continuous batching. All of these sit right at the boundary. They are partly algorithmic ideas and partly systems ideas, and they only work if both sides are designed together.

And honestly, I think there is a deeper intellectual point. Historically, machine learning systems research followed the models. Models came first, systems caught up. What I see now is the arrow starting to point in both directions. Constraints from the system are shaping what architectures people explore. Long-context models, state-space models, linear attention variants, sparsity. A lot of that work is motivated by asking, what would a model look like if it were designed to be efficient from day one? That is co-design in the truest sense.

So from my perspective, it is not that co-design is nice to have. It is that the alternative, treating the model as fixed and the system as an afterthought, simply stops working at this scale. The people who will make the most progress over the next few years are going to be the ones who can hold both the math and the machine in their heads at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response says model-level decisions determine what is possible at the system level and gives GPU-focused examples, including GPU memory hierarchy and attention design.

r002.rationale: It argues that model and system design must work together at large-model scale, citing hardware constraints, serving, and the need for system support to run and scale models.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that, as models get larger, the model and the system become much harder to think about independently. You can design a model that looks very efficient in terms of the number of operations, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it will run efficiently. You also have to consider how much data moves between memory and compute, how the computation is distributed across devices, and how much communication that requires.

And those system costs affect which model designs are practical. For example, if you change the numerical precision or the attention mechanism, you’re making a modeling decision, but you’re also changing what the compiler and hardware need to support. The benefit really depends on both sides working together.

So rather than designing a model first and then asking the systems people to make it fast, we need a feedback loop. What can the system execute well? What changes can we make to the model while preserving quality? In the large-model era, that joint optimization becomes increasingly important because the costs of training and serving are so significant.

r001.rationale: The response discusses efficient execution, memory movement, devices, and hardware, but does not identify GPUs specifically.

r002.rationale: It says that as models get larger, model and system design become harder to separate and that joint optimization is increasingly important, identifying systems support as necessary for large-model scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key reason is that, at this scale, the model and the system become very tightly coupled. The model architecture determines how much computation, memory, and communication you need, and the system determines which of those choices you can actually execute efficiently.

For example, a model might require fewer arithmetic operations but move much more data. On real hardware, that can make it slower. Or you might use a lower-precision representation to reduce memory requirements, but then you need to consider both model quality and whether the underlying system can take advantage of it.

So you need a feedback loop. You make a model choice, understand its behavior on the system, and use that information to revisit the choice. That becomes increasingly necessary as we try to make large models both more capable and more accessible under practical resource constraints.

r001.rationale: The response discusses efficient execution on real hardware, but it does not specifically identify GPUs.

r002.rationale: It says model–system co-design becomes increasingly necessary for large models and explains that system capabilities determine what can be executed efficiently under resource constraints.
